    in the World 2026



           Introduction: About State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World (SOFI)

        Key Findings of the SOFI 2026 Report

      Introduction: About State of Food Security and Nutrition in
     the World (SOFI)

                    It is the UN system’s flagship assessment of global hunger, food insecurity and
             malnutrition.

           Released by: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO),

          Produced jointly by FAO, along with the International

             Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD)

               United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF)

              World Food Programme (WFP)

              World Health Organization (WHO),

                    It tracks progress toward SDG 2 through the latest global and regional estimates on food
             insecurity, diet quality and the global nutrition targets, while offering evidence‑based
             insights that shape policies and investments across the food system. Each edition
            provides governments, development partners and donors with authoritative guidance
          on where action and resources are most urgently needed to reduce hunger and improve
              nutrition.

     Key Findings of the SOFI 2026 Report


                                                            Global hunger continued its gradual decline in
                                                     2025, marking sustained improvement after the
           Overall Status (Global Hunger)                   surge during recent crises. However, progress
                                                        remains insufficient to eliminate hunger by 2030,
                                                             with Africa emerging as the region most affected.





State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026                                                                                          1

An estimated 7.8% of the global population
          Global Hunger Prevalence                       experienced hunger in 2025, down from 8.1% in
                                              2024 and 8.6% in 2022.

                                                   Between 608 and 696 million people (point
                                                               estimate: 645 million) faced hunger in 2025,
          People Facing Hunger
                                                            representing a decline of 14 million compared to
                                              2024 and 43 million compared to 2022.

                                                           Despite continued improvement, an estimated
        2030 Hunger Projection                      510–520 million people may still face hunger by
                                                    2030, with 56% expected to live in Africa.

                                                        Asia and Latin America & the Caribbean
                                                        recorded steady progress in reducing hunger,
          Regional Trends
                                                             while the long-standing rise in hunger in Africa
                                              came to a halt in 2025.

                                                           For the first time, Africa hosted the largest
                                                  number of hungry people, with 309 million,
           Africa Becomes the Most Affected Region
                                                  compared to 292 million in Asia and 32 million in
                                                               Latin America & the Caribbean.

                                                    Hunger affected 20.0% of Africa's population,
          Regional Hunger Rates (2025)                 compared to 6.0% in Asia and 4.8% in Latin
                                                      America & the Caribbean.

                                                                      In 2025, around 2.1 billion people (25.8% of the
                                                            global population) experienced moderate or
         Food Insecurity
                                                       severe food insecurity, down from 28.7% in
                                                    2020.

                                                          Nearly 86 million fewer people experienced food
         Improvement in Food Security                      insecurity in 2025 compared to 2024, and 135
                                                                 million fewer compared to 2020.

                                                         Since 2020, food security improved steadily in
                                                        Asia and Latin America & the Caribbean, while
          Regional Progress in Food Security                Africa recorded its first improvement in 2025
                                                            since the launch of the 2030 Agenda for
                                                         Sustainable Development (2015).

                                                   Moderate and severe food insecurity remained
          Urban–Rural Disparities                           highest in rural areas, lower in peri-urban areas,
                                                   and lowest in urban areas.

                                                   Food insecurity remained higher among women
         Gender Gap in Food Security                    than men, although the gender gap narrowed
                                                                        slightly in 2025 compared to 2024.

          Dietary Diversity                                 Global dietary diversity remains inadequate. Only
                                              30.8% of children (6–23 months) and 62.7% of





State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026                                                                                          2

women (15–49 years) consumed a minimally
                                                          diverse diet.

                                                         Progress in improving maternal and child
          Maternal and Child Nutrition                        nutrition remains too slow to achieve the 2030
                                                                 nutrition targets.

                                                      Improvements in stunting, wasting, overweight
                                             among children under five, low birth weight, and
           Child Nutrition Indicators
                                                           exclusive breastfeeding have been only
                                                         marginal and remain off track.

                                                 Anaemia among women aged 15–49 years
         Anaemia Among Women                         continues to worsen, reversing progress in
                                                          maternal nutrition.

                                                             Accelerating progress requires strengthening
                                                      food systems, improving nutrition-sensitive
                                                                agriculture, expanding social protection,
                                                        promoting healthy and diverse diets, reducing
       Way Forward
                                                      food insecurity, addressing regional and gender
                                                                  disparities, and increasing investments in
                                                        maternal and child nutrition, particularly in
                                                            Africa and other vulnerable regions.


                                                            Global progress towards nutrition and healthy
                                                                 diet targets remains uneven. Rising obesity,
                                                                persistent malnutrition, increasing diet costs,
           Overall Status (Global Nutrition & Healthy Diets)
                                                   and unequal affordability continue to threaten the
                                                       achievement of SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and the
                                              2030 Global Nutrition Targets.

                                                  The global prevalence of adult obesity increased
                                                                  steadily from 12.1% in 2012 to 16.2% in 2024,
          Adult Obesity
                                                          missing the target of halting the rise in obesity by
                                                     2025.

                                                         Progress towards the 2030 Global Nutrition
                                                         Targets varies considerably across regions, with
          Regional Nutrition Progress
                                               some indicators improving while others continue
                                                                  to deteriorate.

                                                  The prevalence of child stunting is declining
           Child Stunting                                         significantly in Africa and is on track to achieve
                                                            the 2030 target in Asia.

                                                          Exclusive breastfeeding rates have improved
                                                         across all regions for which data are available,
          Exclusive Breastfeeding
                                                           supporting better maternal and child health
                                                       outcomes.





State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026                                                                                          3

Nearly all regions are witnessing a widening gap
                                                   between current trends and the 2030 target for
         Anaemia in Women
                                                          reducing anaemia among women aged 15–49
                                                            years.

                                                           Child overweight is increasing rapidly in
           Child Overweight                              Oceania, posing an emerging public health
                                                              challenge.

                                                          Achieving global nutrition targets requires
                                                             stronger multisectoral policies, sustained public
        Need for Multisectoral Action                     investment, and coordinated action across health,
                                                                   agriculture, education, and social protection
                                                               sectors.

                                                    Access to healthy diets is fundamental to
                                                            achieving SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), yet remains
          Healthy Diets & SDG 2
                                                          economically unaffordable for a large share of the
                                                               global population.

                                                  The Cost of a Healthy Diet (CoHD) increased
                                                                 globally from PPP $2.94 (2017) to PPP $3.44
         Cost of Healthy Diet (CoHD)                      (2021) and further to PPP $4.28 (2025) due to
                                                                persistent food price and cost-of-living
                                                             pressures.

                                                               Latin America & the Caribbean recorded the
          Highest Diet Cost                               highest Cost of a Healthy Diet, at PPP $4.91 in
                                                     2025.

                                                  The number of people unable to afford a healthy
                                                                    diet declined from 2.97 billion (37.4%) in 2021 to
           Affordability of Healthy Diets                   2.69 billion (32.7%) in 2025, indicating that
                                                    income growth generally outpaced food price
                                                              increases.

                                                                    Affordability worsened in Africa, where 66.6% of
                                                         the population could not afford a healthy diet in
          Regional Affordability Gap
                                             2025—more than twice the proportion observed
                                                                        in Asia and Latin America & the Caribbean.

                                                      Animal-source foods, fruits, and vegetables
                                                       account for the largest share of healthy diet
         Cost Drivers of Healthy Diets                       costs, while starchy staples contribute relatively
                                                                                              little. The most expensive food group varies
                                                         across regions.





State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026                                                                                          4

Animal-source foods are the costliest
                                                   component of healthy diets in Africa, whereas
          Regional Cost Composition
                                                        vegetables account for the largest share of diet
                                                           costs in Latin America & the Caribbean.

                                                             Differences in food basket composition, food
                                                               prices, and the availability of low-cost local
                                                      foods explain variations in healthy diet costs
         Cross-Country Variation
                                                         across countries. Greater food diversity can
                                                                  substantially reduce the Cost of a Healthy Diet
                                                      (CoHD).

                                                  The CoHD indicator, based on data from the
                                                               International Comparison Programme (ICP),
                                                            estimates the minimum cost of a nutritionally
        CoHD Indicator
                                                      adequate diet using the least-cost available
                                                           foods, though its usefulness is constrained by
                                                                    limited data coverage and update frequency.

                                                          United Nations agencies are supporting countries
                                                                        in producing national CoHD estimates using
          National Monitoring
                                                                         retail food price data, enabling more accurate
                                                   and context-specific monitoring.

                                                  The cost of a healthy diet varies significantly
                                                         across locations and seasons within countries.
          Within-Country Price Variation                    National averages may mask local disparities,
                                                                  highlighting the need for frequent, granular food
                                                            price data.

                                                          Achieving global nutrition goals requires reducing
                                                            the cost of healthy diets, improving food
                                                                   affordability, promoting nutrition-sensitive
                                                                  policies, addressing regional inequalities,
       Way Forward
                                                            strengthening food price monitoring, expanding
                                                               social protection, and increasing investments in
                                                        maternal and child nutrition, sustainable food
                                                         systems, and healthy food production.


                                                       Lowering the Cost of a Healthy Diet (CoHD)
                                                              requires transforming agrifood systems through
           Overall Status (Reducing the Cost of Healthy      higher productivity, efficient value chains, better
           Diets)                                                 infrastructure, supportive policies, and targeted
                                                            investments. Context-specific interventions are
                                                  more effective than one-size-fits-all approaches.

          Agrifood System Characteristics               Lower CoHD is associated with higher
                                                                agricultural productivity, improved crop yields,
                                                              greater public investment in agricultural





State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026                                                                                          5

research & development (R&D), efficient
                                                           transport and logistics, better road
                                                                infrastructure, higher mobile connectivity,
                                                             stronger trade integration, and lower electricity
                                                 and labour costs.

                                                      Reducing diet costs requires two complementary
                                                                   strategies: (i) expanding the supply of nutritious
           Policy Approaches                            foods through domestic production and trade,
                                                   and (ii) lowering structural costs across the
                                                             agrifood value chain.

                                                  The greatest reductions in diet costs are achieved
                                                         through combined investments in agricultural
                                                   R&D, irrigation, transport infrastructure, cold-
           Integrated Investment Strategy
                                                        chain facilities, food loss reduction, and reforms
                                                                        in subsidy policies, trade facilitation, and
                                                           regulatory frameworks.

                                                      Long-term productivity gains are highest when
                                                                    agricultural R&D focuses on fruits, vegetables,
           Agricultural Research & Development (R&D)
                                                 and legumes, which are essential components of
                                                             healthy diets.

                                                                Productivity gains translate into affordable diets
                                                            only when supported by quality seed systems,
          Enabling Systems for Technology Adoption       water management, secure land tenure, access
                                                              to finance, and agricultural extension services
                                                                   that promote technology adoption.

                                                       Post-farmgate activities account for 70–75% of
                                                         the final consumer price of food, with up to 40%
         Importance of Post-Farmgate Activities
                                                            of value chain costs arising from processing,
                                                                   logistics, and wholesale operations.

                                                       Enhancing efficiency in processing, storage,
                                                              transport, and distribution is critical for reducing
          Improving Value Chain Efficiency                 the prices of perishable and nutritious foods,
                                                                    particularly fruits, vegetables, and animal-source
                                                             foods.

                                                         Coordinated improvements across the entire
                                                          agrifood value chain deliver significantly greater
           Integrated Value Chain Interventions
                                                            reductions in healthy diet costs than isolated
                                                                  interventions.

          Regional Priorities                                     Priority interventions include expanding cold-
                                                        chain infrastructure and reducing animal-source
                                                      food costs in Africa, improving transport
                                                   systems and lowering vegetable prices in Latin





State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026                                                                                          6

America & the Caribbean, and strengthening
                                                         post-harvest handling of fruits in Asia.

                                                              Public expenditure is most effective when
                                                              directed towards high-cost nutritious food
          Targeted Public Spending                       groups, whereas broad subsidies on already low-
                                                         cost staple foods have limited impact on
                                                          improving overall diet affordability.

                                                           Cost-reduction reforms should ensure that
                                                          increased efficiency does not compromise
         Governance Challenges
                                                        environmental sustainability, public health, or
                                                     decent rural livelihoods.

                                                  Demand-side interventions should be carefully
                                                           coordinated with expanding food supply to
         Sequencing of Reforms
                                                           prevent unintended increases in food prices and
                                                        ensure stable markets.

                                                         Since agrifood reforms have redistributive
                                                                 effects, governments should provide transition
           Inclusive Transition                             support, strengthen public–private partnerships,
                                                   and ensure that smallholder farmers, women,
                                                 and youth benefit from agrifood transformation.

                                                    Making healthy diets affordable requires
                                                             increasing agricultural productivity,
                                                            strengthening value chains, investing in R&D,
                                                                infrastructure, and cold chains, improving trade
       Way Forward                              and market efficiency, targeting high-cost
                                                                nutritious foods, and implementing inclusive,
                                                            sustainable, and well-governed agrifood
                                                       reforms that benefit both consumers and
                                                           producers.
